questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the term "es<d&eaMyh" used for the water-carrier woman in the story, and what ironic contrast does this name create with her actual role?
questions.a: Literally, "es<d&eaMyh" means "small mother" or "little mother" — a diminutive, affectionate term. Ironically, she performs the massive, life-sustaining labor of supplying water to entire households, making her role anything but "small." A wrong answer (e.g., "it's just a name") reveals the student misses how Sahni uses naming as verbal irony: society diminishes her stature while depending on her survival labor.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the leather water-bag (dhpM+) functions as a symbol at two different levels in the story.
questions.a: At the literal level, the dhpM+ is the tool of the water-carrier's trade — a heavy leather bag carried on the head to transport water. At the symbolic level, it represents the crushing weight of systemic poverty: the bag never empties completely, just as their struggle never ends; it leaks (like their dignity under social pressure); yet they carry it with straightened backs. A wrong answer that only describes the physical bag shows the student cannot move from concrete object to abstract meaning — the core skill of symbol analysis.

questions.q: Apply the concept of situational irony to the scene where the narrator offers the water-carrier woman water from his own supply, and she refuses saying "ns[k Hkb;k :B er" (look, I've filled my bag). What makes this situation ironic?
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when outcome contradicts expectation. The narrator expects gratitude from a "needy" person; instead, the woman asserts self-reliance — she has already secured water through her own labor. The irony deepens: the "giver" is emotionally empty (guilt-ridden, conflicted), while the "receiver" is morally full (dignified, autonomous). A wrong answer focusing only on plot ("she said no") misses the role-reversal that exposes charity as performance.

questions.q: Analyze how the recurring motif of "night" (dkys) operates as both setting and symbol in the story's opening and closing sections. What relationship does it establish between time and oppression?
questions.a: The opening "dkys es?kk ikuh ns" (dark night, give me light/water) frames night as active agent of suffering — the time when water scarcity bites hardest, when the poor walk miles in darkness. By the end, night becomes symbolic of structural blindness: the privileged sleep through the crisis they create. The relationship: night is not neutral time but allocated time — the poor's labor-time, the rich's ignorance-time. A wrong answer treating night as mere backdrop fails to see how Sahni makes setting do ideological work.

questions.q: Evaluate this interpretation: "The story's central irony is that the water-carriers are called 'es<d&eaMyh' (small) but possess 'cM+h' (large) moral stature, while the narrator is physically 'cM+h' but morally 'es<d'." Defend or challenge with two textual anchors.
questions.a: The interpretation holds. Textual anchor 1: The narrator admits "mez esa esjh ek¡ ls Hkh cM+h Fkha" (she was bigger than even my mother) — explicit moral sizing. Anchor 2: The woman's refusal "ge bUgsa ikuh ugha nsaxs rks banz Hkxoku gesa ikuh oSQls nsaxs" (if you don't give us water, will the rich give us water?) — she names the structural truth the narrator evades. A wrong answer that calls this "theme not irony" confuses the device (ironic inversion of size/stature) with the idea it serves.

questions.q: Create a 4-line poetic response from the water-carrier woman's perspective that uses one symbol from the story (dhpM+, ikuh, dkys, or rat) and one ironic twist. Write in Hindi or English.
questions.a:
Example (Hindi):
dhpM+ bhari, sar uncha, raat bhi hai saath
ikuh mangne wale, ab dete hain haath
(translation: Bag full, head high, night too is with me / Those who begged for water, now extend hands)
Criteria: Must use a story symbol concretely + flip an expectation (beggar becomes giver, night becomes ally). A poor answer uses the symbol decoratively without irony (e.g., "my bag is heavy, night is dark") — showing the student cannot wield devices creatively.
